title: Reinspection Request
tips: Name the specific items in dispute — don't just ask for "another look." Attach documentation in the same message.

title: Reinspection Follow-Up
body:
Hi {{adjuster_name}},

Following up on the reinspection request I sent on {{original_request_date}} for {{client_name}} ({{claim_number}}). Do you have a date we can lock in? Let me know if you need anything else from us to get it scheduled.

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Ask for a firm date, not just confirmation it's "in progress."

title: Appraisal Demand Follow-Up
body:
Hi {{adjuster_name}},

Following up on the appraisal demand we sent on {{demand_date}} for {{client_name}} ({{claim_number}}). Can you confirm your selected appraiser so we can move forward? Let me know if there's anything outstanding on our end.

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Keep this short — you're just confirming their appraiser is named and the clock is moving.

title: Adjuster Follow-Up (General)
body:
Hi {{adjuster_name}},

Following up on {{claim_number}} for {{client_name}} — specifically on {{what_you_need}}. It's been {{time_elapsed}} since my last message. Can you give me an update, or let me know if you need anything further from us?

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: State exactly what you're waiting on and how long it's been — this makes the pattern clear if you need to escalate later.

title: Appraiser Follow-Up
body:
Hi {{appraiser_name}},

Checking in on {{claim_number}} for {{client_name}}. It's been about {{time_elapsed}} since our last update — is there anything new on your end, or anything you need from us to keep things moving?

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: 2-3 weeks without an update is the standard trigger for this follow-up during active appraisal.

title: Documentation Request (to client or vendor)
tips: Explain why you need it, briefly — people respond faster to a request that makes sense to them.

title: Client Follow-Up (General)
body:
Hi {{client_name}},

Just following up on {{what_you_need}} for your claim ({{claim_number}}). We're ready to move forward once we have this — let me know if you have any questions or if now's not a good time, and we can find something that works.

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Keep it warm, not just a repeat of the same ask — invite a response.

title: Client Explanation of Appraisal
body:
Hi {{client_name}},

I wanted to walk you through the next step in your claim. Because {{carrier_name}}'s estimate and ours are far enough apart, we're going to invoke something called appraisal — it's a process built into your policy for exactly this kind of disagreement.

Here's how it works: each side picks an independent appraiser to review the damage, and if the two appraisers don't agree, a neutral third person called an umpire settles the difference. This isn't a sign anything has gone wrong — it's a normal, contractual way to resolve a disagreement on scope or pricing.

I'll keep you updated at each step. Do you have any questions before we move forward?

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Avoid promising a specific timeline or outcome — keep it to the mechanics and next steps.

title: Client Stalled-Claim Message
body:
Hi {{client_name}},

I know this claim has been taking longer than either of us would like. Here's where things actually stand: {{current_status}}. Here's what we're doing next: {{next_step}}.

I'll keep you posted as soon as there's an update — feel free to reach out anytime with questions.

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Lead with facts, not just reassurance — clients respond well to knowing exactly where things stand.

title: Internal Escalation Message
body:
Hi {{lead_name}},

I need your input on {{claim_number}} ({{client_name}}). Quick summary: {{situation_summary}}.

What we've tried so far: {{what_tried}}.

What I need from you: {{specific_ask}}.

Happy to hop on a call if that's faster.

Thanks,
{{your_name}}
tips: Lead with the specific ask — a lead reading a dozen of these a week will thank you for not burying it.

title: ITEL Rebuttal – Illinois "No Matching Coverage" Denial (Allstate)
tips: Lead with the policy language and the ITEL finding. Before sending: (1) paste the exact replacement cost / like kind and quality wording from this insured's Allstate policy form; (2) confirm the insured's written authorization. Illinois restricts contractors from negotiating claims for an insured, so send this from the insured, or with their sign-off, if your compliance team requires it. Do NOT claim that Illinois has a matching statute or regulation; it does not. The argument is contractual. Keep the tone factual. If the adjuster repeats "no matching in Illinois," use the second-round letter (illinois-no-matching-second-rebuttal).

title: Second-Round Rebuttal – Adjuster Repeats "No Matching in Illinois" (Full Position Letter)
body:
Re: Second Request for Reconsideration and Written Coverage Position – Claim {{claim_number}}
Insured: {{client_name}}
Property: {{property_address}}
Date of Loss: {{date_of_loss}}
Policy No.: {{policy_number}} (Form {{policy_form_number}})

To: {{adjuster_name}}
cc: {{adjuster_supervisor_name}}, Claims Supervisor / Manager

{{adjuster_name}},

On {{first_rebuttal_date}} we asked Allstate to reconsider limiting the roof scope to {{approved_scope}}, and we submitted ITEL report #{{itel_report_number}}. Allstate's response of {{second_denial_date}} again said that "Illinois has no matching law / matching policy." It did not identify any language in the insured's policy, and it did not address the ITEL findings. Because this is the second time, we are copying your supervisor and setting out our position in full. We ask that Allstate respond to each point in writing.

1. We agree that Illinois has no matching statute. That does not decide this claim.

Some states have a statute or regulation that specifically requires insurers to match. Illinois does not, and we are not relying on one. A state statute sets a minimum standard for claims handling. It does not define, and cannot shrink, what the insurer agreed to in its own contract. Allstate's obligation here comes from the policy it sold to {{client_name}}. The policy contains no exclusion that says "Allstate will not pay to achieve a reasonable match." The absence of a matching statute is not a policy exclusion, and Allstate cannot add one now by pointing to what the legislature has not done.

The question is not "Does Illinois require matching?" The question is "What does Allstate's replacement cost promise require on this roof, given that the original shingle is no longer made?"

2. What the policy promises.

The insured's policy provides:

"{{exact_policy_replacement_cost_language}}"
[Quote verbatim from the declarations and policy form, with page and section: for example, the replacement cost / Building Structure Reimbursement provision and any "like kind and quality," "equivalent construction," or "comparable material and quality" language.]

Replacement cost coverage exists to put the insured back in the position they were in before the loss, with property of like kind and quality, without a deduction for the difference between old and new. Before this storm, the insured had a roof with a uniform color, profile, and exposure. A repair with a visibly different shingle leaves the insured with something less. That is not "like kind and quality." It is a different, lesser roof that the insured did not have before the loss.

3. The ITEL evidence is specific, independent, and unrebutted.

ITEL report #{{itel_report_number}} ({{itel_report_date}}) analyzed a physical sample taken from this roof at {{sample_location}}. It found:
- Existing product: {{existing_product_identification}}
- Status: {{itel_status_finding}} (for example: discontinued; no longer manufactured)
- Closest available product: {{closest_match_product}}
- How it differs: {{mismatch_specifics}} (for example: color blend, granule, dimensions, exposure, profile/dimensional pattern)
{{optional_repairability_finding}}
[If ITEL or a brittleness test shows that the existing shingles cannot be lifted, removed, or re-sealed without damage, say so here. That means a "repair" cannot be done at all without damaging the surrounding undamaged roof.]

ITEL is a third-party laboratory. Neither the contractor nor the insured selected its conclusions. Allstate has not provided any contrary report, product identification, or test. An adjuster's opinion that a product "should match" or "will weather in" is not evidence that a matching product exists. If Allstate believes a matching product is available, it should identify the manufacturer, product line, color, and a current supplier, so the insured can buy it.

4. How courts applying Illinois law read this language.

The Seventh Circuit, applying Illinois law, addressed this issue in Windridge of Naperville Condominium Ass'n v. Philadelphia Indemnity Insurance Co., 932 F.3d 1035 (7th Cir. 2019). There, a storm damaged siding on two sides of the buildings, and matching siding was no longer available. The court affirmed judgment for the insured: the insurer had to pay to replace the siding on all sides, including the undamaged sides, so the result matched. The court reasoned that the replacement cost promise is meant to restore the insured to its pre-loss position, and a building with mismatched siding does not do that. The court noted that a trivial mismatch might not require full replacement. This mismatch is not trivial: {{why_mismatch_is_substantial}} [for example: the replacement product is a different color blend and dimensional profile on the street-facing elevation, plainly visible from the street].

Two settled rules of Illinois insurance law also apply:
- Policy language is construed against the insurer that drafted it, and any ambiguity is resolved in favor of coverage (Outboard Marine Corp. v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., 154 Ill. 2d 90 (1992)). If Allstate reads "like kind and quality" to allow a visibly mismatched roof, that reading must give way to the reasonable reading that the restored roof must be of comparable appearance.
- The insurer bears the burden of proving that an exclusion or limitation applies (Addison Insurance Co. v. Fay, 232 Ill. 2d 446 (2009)). Allstate has not identified any exclusion. "No matching law" does not meet that burden.

5. A roof is not divisible into unrelated pieces.

Shingle roofs are an interlocking system. Courses overlap, sealant strips bond each course to the next, and the color and pattern read as one surface. Replacing {{approved_scope}} with a discontinued-product substitute creates a visible patch on a single, continuous surface. That patch reduces the property's appearance and value, and it is exactly the kind of loss replacement cost coverage is meant to restore.

6. Allstate's claim-handling obligations.

Illinois regulations require that when an insurer denies all or part of a first-party claim, it give a reasonable written explanation that clearly sets forth the specific policy definition, limitation, exclusion, or condition on which the denial is based, together with the notice of availability of the Illinois Department of Insurance. (50 Ill. Adm. Code 919.50(a)(1)) A statement that "Illinois has no matching law" identifies no policy provision at all. Illinois law also requires a reasonable investigation based on all available information before a claim is denied, which includes the ITEL report (see 215 ILCS 5/154.6).

7. What we are asking Allstate to do.

Within {{response_days}} days, please do one of the following.

(a) Revise the estimate to include {{requested_scope}} so the restored roof has a reasonably uniform appearance consistent with like kind and quality.

OR

(b) Provide a written coverage position that:
   1. quotes the specific policy language (form number, page, section) Allstate relies on to limit the scope;
   2. explains how Allstate considered ITEL report #{{itel_report_number}}, and identifies any contrary evidence Allstate relied on;
   3. identifies the specific product (manufacturer, line, color, supplier) that Allstate contends is a match, if it contends one exists; and
   4. includes the Department of Insurance notice of availability required by 919.50.

We also ask that {{adjuster_supervisor_name}} review the file, and that Allstate keep all claim notes, estimates, photos, and communications related to this claim.

8. Reservation of rights.

The insured reserves all rights under the policy and Illinois law. That includes invoking the policy's appraisal provision to resolve the amount of loss, and filing a complaint with the Illinois Department of Insurance. Nothing in this letter waives any right or remedy.

We would much rather resolve this with Allstate directly. If Allstate's position is that its policy truly excludes restoring a uniform roof, please show us the language and we will review it with the insured. If it cannot show us that language, we ask that the scope be corrected.

Attachments:
- ITEL report #{{itel_report_number}}
- Photos: sample location, damaged area, elevation views showing the visibility of the affected area
- Side-by-side photo of the existing shingle and the closest available product (if available)
- Manufacturer discontinuation notice (if available)
- Contractor estimate for {{requested_scope}}
- Our prior letter of {{first_rebuttal_date}} and Allstate's responses

Sincerely,
{{your_name}}
{{company_name}}
On behalf of and with the written authorization of {{client_name}}
{{client_signature_line_if_required}}
tips: Use this after the first rebuttal (illinois-itel-matching-rebuttal) is refused. Copy the supervisor. Before sending: (1) pull the insured's actual policy form and quote the replacement cost language word for word. Also check for an actual matching/cosmetic exclusion or a roof-surface endorsement. If one exists, do NOT send this letter; escalate internally instead. (2) Describe concretely why the mismatch is not trivial (visible elevation, color/profile difference). (3) Add the repairability finding if you have one; it is often the strongest fact. (4) Get the insured's written authorization or signature, per compliance. (5) The case citations are accurate summaries, but have counsel confirm them before you rely on them in a formal demand. Never say Illinois has a matching statute; it doesn't. Do not threaten 215 ILCS 5/155 penalties in this letter; that's a counsel-level step.
